relations.note: Kai-Kai raises the sea while Tren-Tren raises its mountain to protect refugees.
relations.source: Rosales, Historia general, book I, chapter 1

relations.note: Tren-Tren commands survivors to offer a quartered child partly to Kai-Kai.
relations.source: Rosales, Historia general, book I, chapter 1

relations.note: Sun casts down rebellious children who are later revived as Kai-Kai.
Moon intercedes for her rebellious children, who later become Kai-Kai.
Moon’s grief creates lakes from which Kai-Kai’s aquatic domain develops.
The creator fashions Tren-Tren from special clay and orders it to warn humanity.
Fish-kings consume portions of the child offered to appease the sea powers.
relations.source: Rosales, Historia general, book I, chapter 1

relations.note: Mermaids consume portions of the child cast into the sea as an offering.
relations.source: Rosales, Historia general, book I, chapter 1

relations.note: The catastrophe grounds survivors’ renewed relationship with Chau Ngünechen and the ngillatun.
Some later stories describe pillanes as Kai-Kai’s assistants.
Some later stories make Kai-Kai a descendant or child of pillanes.
Later interpreters structurally relate Tren-Tren’s transformed aquatic survivors to the Sumpall cycle.
Modern pantheon charts classify Kai-Kai among destructive wekufü.
